patient.name: Daniel Okafor
patient.complaint: Sudden breathlessness and sharp right-sided chest pain this morning
background: Flew back from Lagos 5 days ago (7-hour flight after a long drive)
Right calf swollen and sore for 3 days
Bus driver in Lewisham; no previous clots

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia after a flight, surgery or pregnancy, often with a clear chest, a normal CXR and sinus tachycardia; or a collapsed patient with massive PE.

points: Daniel, 47, flew back from **Lagos** 5 days ago.
Right calf swollen and sore for 3 days.
This morning: sudden breathlessness and **sharp right chest pain** on breathing in.
Coughed up a streak of blood.

steps.lead: Daniel's calf clot has most likely travelled to his **pulmonary arteries**. The flight and obesity make it a **provoked** PE.

points: Right calf swollen, tender and pitting.
Chest clear: no crackles, normal percussion.
Heart sounds normal; JVP not raised yet.

steps.lead: Daniel has the full picture: **pleuritic pain**, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypoxia, low-grade fever, haemoptysis, and a swollen calf first.

steps.title: PE vs the other causes of pleuritic pain
head: Feature
PE
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax

steps.q: Which feature in Daniel most points to PE rather than pneumonia?
o: Swollen calf before the chest pain
steps.r: Fever, pleuritic pain and tachypnoea occur in both. A **swollen calf followed by chest symptoms** is the classic PE pattern.

steps.text: **Hypoxia and tachycardia with a clear chest** and a normal CXR: think PE.

visual.title: Systolic BP and massive PE
visual.label: Daniel 128
visual.caption: Daniel is stable for now. Sustained hypotension or collapse changes the whole plan.

steps.lead: Daniel's BP of 128/80 means this is **not yet massive**. Watch for systolic below 90 for over 15 minutes, or collapse.
If Daniel later needs heparin, a falling platelet count with new clots means **HIT**: stop heparin and switch, e.g. to argatroban.

steps.text: A normal chest X-ray does **not** exclude PE. It is usually normal; its job is to exclude other causes.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial/diagnostic investigation?': the 2-level Wells score decides D-dimer (4 or less) versus CTPA (more than 4), with V/Q scan when CTPA is unsuitable. Also 'most likely ECG/ABG finding'.

steps.title: 2-level Wells pathway for PE
nodes: Suspected PE: calculate the 2-level Wells score
CTPA unsuitable (pregnancy, AKI, iodine allergy) → V/Q scan
D-dimer positive → CTPA; negative → PE excluded

steps.q: Daniel has clinical DVT signs, PE is the most likely diagnosis, and his HR is 112. What is his Wells score?
steps.r: **DVT signs 3 + PE most likely 3 + HR >100 1.5 = 7.5.** Above 4, so PE likely.

visual.title: 2-level Wells score for PE
visual.label: Daniel 7.5
visual.caption: PE likely: straight to imaging, no D-dimer.

steps.lead: Daniel scores **7.5: PE likely**, so he goes straight to **CTPA**, the gold-standard imaging.
Had Daniel scored 4 or less, a **D-dimer** would come first: negative excludes PE, positive leads to CTPA.
Daniel fails **PERC** (HR 112, SpO2 92%, swollen leg), so PE cannot be ruled out at the bedside. **PESI** later decides outpatient care.

steps.title: Arterial blood gas on air and bloods
steps.text: Low PaO2, low PaCO2, high pH: **respiratory alkalosis** from hyperventilation. Troponin and BNP rise with right heart strain.

visual.title: Daniel's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Sinus tachycardia with T inversion in III and V1–V3: right heart strain. A deep S in I and Q in III would complete S1Q3T3.

visual.title: Daniel's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Clear lung fields. Usually normal in PE, but it excludes pneumothorax and pneumonia.

steps.lead: Daniel's normal CXR, **sinus tachycardia** with T inversion in V1–V3 and respiratory alkalosis all fit PE with right heart strain.

points: Filling defects in **both main pulmonary arteries**.

steps.lead: Daniel's CTPA was immediate. If pregnant with leg signs: **duplex USS** first. If scanning is delayed: interim **rivaroxaban**.

steps.text: Do not send a D-dimer when Wells is **above 4**. A negative D-dimer cannot exclude PE in a high-probability patient.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': thrombolysis (alteplase) for the hypotensive patient, a DOAC for the stable one, outpatient rivaroxaban for low PESI, and UFH or LMWH in special cases.

points: Back from CTPA, Daniel **collapses** on the trolley.
BP **82/50 mmHg** for 20 minutes despite fluids.
JVP raised to the earlobe; parasternal heave.

steps.q: Daniel has a confirmed PE and is now persistently hypotensive. What is the next step?
steps.r: Persistent hypotension = **massive PE**: thrombolyse. Embolectomy is only if thrombolysis is unsuitable.

steps.lead: ABCDE, 15 L oxygen, then **IV alteplase with IV UFH**. Daniel has no CNS bleed, recent surgery, trauma or bleeding disorder.

visual.title: Daniel after alteplase
visual.caption: Thrombolysis breaks up the clot, RV afterload falls and the BP recovers.

steps.title: PE management by severity
nodes: Thrombolysis unsuitable → embolectomy or catheter therapy

steps.lead: Once stable, Daniel moves to a **DOAC**. LMWH, warfarin with LMWH bridging, or UFH are for special cases.
Daniel's PE was **provoked** by the journey, so at least **3 months**. Antiphospholipid syndrome would mean lifelong warfarin.
Daniel's care follows **NICE NG158**, with Wells, PERC and the BTS-backed **PESI** guiding tests and where he is treated.

steps.text: Do not thrombolyse a **stable** patient. Alteplase is for hypotension or collapse; its bleeding risk is serious.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why PE causes hypoxaemia with a low PaCO2, why it causes obstructive shock, and why S1Q3T3 or T inversion in V1–V3 appear.

steps.title: From leg to lung
nodes: Virchow's triad → DVT in the calf
Clot embolises via the IVC and right heart
Ventilated but unperfused lung: V/Q mismatch

steps.lead: Daniel's calf clot formed from **stasis** on the journey, with obesity adding to it: **Virchow's triad**.
Daniel's PaO2 8.1 and PaCO2 3.9 are **V/Q mismatch** plus hyperventilation: a respiratory alkalosis.

steps.r: Hypoxia and lung receptors drive **hyperventilation**, which blows off CO2: respiratory alkalosis.

steps.title: Why Daniel collapsed
nodes: RV afterload rises → RV dilates and fails

steps.lead: Daniel's collapse is **obstructive shock**: the clot raised pulmonary resistance until his right ventricle failed.
Daniel's T inversion in V1–V3 is his **strained right ventricle**, the same reason S1Q3T3 appears.

steps.text: S1Q3T3 is classic but **uncommon**. The most likely ECG finding in PE is **sinus tachycardia**.

mcq.q: Which acid-base disturbance is typical of PE?
mcq.r: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2: **respiratory alkalosis**, with a low PaO2.

o: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg for over 15 minutes
mcq.r: **Persistent hypotension <90 mmHg for >15 minutes**, or collapse.

mcq.q: Which drug replaces heparin in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?
mcq.r: Stop heparin and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant such as **argatroban**.

mcq.q: What is the next test when the 2-level PE Wells score is 4 or less?
mcq.r: **D-dimer** first: negative excludes PE; positive means CTPA.

mcq.q: Which imaging is used when CTPA is unsuitable, e.g. in AKI or iodine allergy?
Which is the most common ECG finding in PE?
mcq.r: **Sinus tachycardia**. S1Q3T3 is classic but less common.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for a massive PE?
mcq.r: **Thrombolysis with alteplase (or tenecteplase) plus IV UFH.** Embolectomy if thrombolysis is unsuitable.

mcq.q: Which anticoagulant is used for PE in end-stage renal failure?
mcq.r: **UFH** is third-line, for severe renal insufficiency or ESRF.

mcq.q: How long is anticoagulation in antiphospholipid syndrome after PE?
mcq.r: **Lifelong warfarin**, starting with LMWH until INR 2–3.
Ventilated but unperfused lung units: **V/Q mismatch**.

prompts.q: What is a PE and what are its provoking risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: find the one risk factor the stem hides.

points.p: A clot in the pulmonary arteries, usually a DVT embolised from the leg
points.why: Look for the swollen calf in the stem.

points.p: Recent surgery, immobility, long-haul flight
points.why: Surgery in the last few weeks counts.

points.p: Pregnancy or postpartum; COCP or HRT
points.why: Pregnancy also changes which scan you use.

points.p: Cancer, previous VTE, thrombophilia, obesity
points.why: Cancer extends treatment to 6 months.

points.p: Antiphospholipid syndrome
points.why: Means lifelong warfarin.

prompts.q: How does PE present, including the signs of right heart strain?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: sudden, pleuritic, hypoxic, with a clear chest.

points.p: Sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain
points.why: The commonest presenting pair.

points.p: Tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypoxia
points.why: Hypoxia out of proportion to the chest findings.

points.p: Haemoptysis, syncope, low-grade fever
points.why: Low-grade fever can mislead you towards pneumonia.

points.p: Signs of DVT: swollen painful calf
points.why: Swollen calf then chest symptoms is the classic pattern.

points.p: Right heart strain: raised JVP, parasternal heave, loud P2
points.why: These suggest a large clot.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the BP decides thrombolysis.

points.p: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg
points.why: Shock from RV failure.

points.p: For more than 15 minutes, or collapse
points.why: Transient dips do not count.

points.p: With RV strain
points.why: Bedside echo shows a dilated RV.

prompts.q: Which complication of PE treatment lowers the platelets, and how is it managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: heparin a few days ago + falling platelets + new clots.

points.p: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
points.why: Typically 5 to 10 days after starting heparin.

points.p: Stop heparin promptly and get haematology review
points.why: Do not give platelets or more heparin.

points.p: Switch to argatroban
points.why: A non-heparin direct thrombin inhibitor.

prompts.q: Which conditions mimic PE, and what feature tells you it is PE instead?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each mimic has one sign PE lacks.

points.p: Pneumonia: fever, productive cough, crackles, consolidation on CXR
points.why: PE usually has a clear chest and a normal CXR.

points.p: Pneumothorax: reduced breath sounds, hyper-resonance
points.why: The CXR shows absent lung markings.

points.p: ACS: central crushing pain, ST changes
points.why: PE pain is pleuritic.

points.p: Pericarditis: pain eased sitting forward, saddle ST elevation
points.why: Positional pain points away from PE.

prompts.q: Walk through the 2-level Wells pathway for PE, with the scores.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the score decides CTPA or D-dimer.

points.p: Items: PE most likely +3, clinical DVT signs +3, HR >100 +1.5
points.why: Recent surgery or immobilisation also scores 1.5.

points.p: Score >4 (likely): CTPA
points.why: CTPA is the gold-standard imaging.

points.p: Score ≤4 (unlikely): D-dimer first
points.why: Positive → CTPA; negative → PE excluded.

points.p: CTPA unsuitable (pregnancy, AKI, iodine allergy): V/Q scan
points.why: Avoids iodinated contrast.

points.p: Delay to scan: interim treatment-dose anticoagulation
points.why: For example rivaroxaban.

prompts.q: What do the PERC rule and PESI score do?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: PERC rules out; PESI decides the setting.

points.p: PERC excludes PE only if all criteria met
points.why: Age <50, HR <100, SpO2 >94%, no leg swelling, haemoptysis, surgery, VTE or oestrogen.

points.p: PESI identifies low-risk patients
points.why: Recommended by the BTS.

points.p: PESI class 1–2: outpatient rivaroxaban
points.why: Avoids admission for stable, low-risk PE.

prompts.q: What do the CXR, ECG and ABG show in PE?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'most likely finding' means the common one, not the classic one.

points.p: CXR usually normal (excludes other causes)
points.why: A normal CXR with hypoxia is a PE clue.

points.p: ECG: sinus tachycardia most commonly
points.why: The usual right answer to 'most likely ECG finding'.

points.p: S1Q3T3 classic but less common; T inversion V1–V3
points.why: Both reflect RV strain.

points.p: ABG: low PaO2, low PaCO2 (respiratory alkalosis)
points.why: Troponin and BNP may also rise.

prompts.q: How do you manage a massive PE?

points.p: ABCDE with 15 L oxygen via non-rebreathe if hypoxic
points.why: Resuscitate first.

points.p: Thrombolysis: IV alteplase (or tenecteplase)
points.why: First-line for massive or unstable PE.

points.p: Plus IV unfractionated heparin
points.why: UFH can be stopped quickly if bleeding.

points.p: Contraindications: CNS bleed, recent trauma or surgery, bleeding disorder, haemorrhagic stroke ever
points.why: Then consider embolectomy.

points.p: If thrombolysis unsuitable: embolectomy or catheter intervention
points.why: A specialist procedure.

prompts.q: How do you anticoagulate a stable PE, and for how long?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: drug by situation, then duration by cause.

points.p: First-line DOAC: apixaban or rivaroxaban
points.why: For stable patients with normal renal function.

points.p: LMWH if DOAC unsuitable (pregnancy, cancer, renal impairment)
points.why: LMWH is the choice in pregnancy.

points.p: UFH in severe renal failure / ESRF
points.why: Third-line.

points.p: Provoked: at least 3 months; active cancer: 6 months
points.why: Unprovoked may need longer.

points.p: Antiphospholipid syndrome: lifelong warfarin
points.why: Recurrence on warfarin: target INR 3–4.

prompts.q: Why does PE cause hypoxaemia, a low PaCO2 and obstructive shock?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: V/Q mismatch for the gas, RV afterload for the shock.

points.p: V/Q mismatch: ventilated but unperfused units
points.why: Bronchoconstricting mediators worsen it.

points.p: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2: respiratory alkalosis
points.why: So a normal or low PaCO2 with hypoxia.

points.p: Raised pulmonary vascular resistance increases RV afterload
points.why: The RV cannot cope with a sudden rise.

points.p: RV strain and failure cause obstructive shock
points.why: Tricuspid regurgitation may appear.

prompts.q: Why do S1Q3T3 and T inversion in V1–V3 appear in PE?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: both ECG signs mean the right ventricle is struggling.

points.p: Acute right ventricular strain
points.why: V1–V3 sit over the right ventricle.

points.p: From the sudden rise in pulmonary vascular resistance
points.why: Rare in small peripheral clots.

glossary.PE: Pulmonary embolism: a clot blocking a pulmonary artery, usually from a leg DVT.
glossary.DVT: Deep vein thrombosis: a clot in a deep leg vein; the usual source of PE.
glossary.VTE: Venous thromboembolism: the umbrella term for DVT and PE.
glossary.massive PE: PE with systolic BP below 90 mmHg for over 15 minutes, or collapse.
glossary.Wells score: A clinical score of PE probability; above 4 means PE likely.
glossary.PERC: Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria; if all eight are met, PE can be excluded without testing.
glossary.PESI: Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index; classes 1 to 2 can be treated as outpatients.
glossary.D-dimer: A fibrin breakdown product; sensitive but not specific, so used to rule PE out.
glossary.CTPA: CT pulmonary angiogram: contrast CT of the pulmonary arteries; the gold-standard test.
glossary.V/Q scan: Ventilation/perfusion scan; shows lung areas that are ventilated but not perfused.
glossary.V/Q mismatch: Air reaching lung units that get no blood flow, so oxygen is not picked up.
glossary.S1Q3T3: Deep S wave in lead I, Q wave and inverted T in lead III; a sign of RV strain.
glossary.right heart strain: Overload of the right ventricle from a sudden rise in pulmonary pressure.
glossary.RV: Right ventricle, which pumps blood into the pulmonary arteries.
glossary.obstructive shock: Shock from a physical block to blood flow, such as a massive PE.
glossary.afterload: The resistance a ventricle must pump against.
glossary.parasternal heave: A lifting impulse beside the sternum from an enlarged right ventricle.
glossary.JVP: Jugular venous pressure; raised when the right heart is failing.
glossary.P2: The pulmonary component of the second heart sound; loud in pulmonary hypertension.
glossary.pleuritic: Sharp chest pain worse on breathing in or coughing.
glossary.respiratory alkalosis: High blood pH from a low PaCO2 caused by breathing too fast.
glossary.PaO2: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood.
glossary.PaCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: measures pH, oxygen and carbon dioxide in arterial blood.
glossary.BNP: B-type natriuretic peptide, released by stretched ventricles.
glossary.troponin: A heart muscle protein released when heart cells are damaged or strained.
glossary.thrombolysis: Drug treatment that dissolves a clot, such as alteplase.
glossary.alteplase: A recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that breaks down clots.
glossary.tenecteplase: A clot-busting tissue plasminogen activator given as a single bolus.
glossary.embolectomy: Surgical or catheter removal of a clot from an artery.
glossary.DOAC: Direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban or rivaroxaban.
glossary.apixaban: A DOAC that directly inhibits factor Xa.
glossary.rivaroxaban: A DOAC that directly inhibits factor Xa; used for outpatient PE treatment.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, a subcutaneous anticoagulant; used in pregnancy.
glossary.UFH: Unfractionated heparin; an IV anticoagulant used in renal failure and with thrombolysis.
glossary.unfractionated heparin: An IV anticoagulant with a short half-life that can be reversed quickly.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio, used to monitor warfarin; target 2 to 3.
glossary.HIT: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: an immune reaction causing low platelets and new clots.
glossary.argatroban: A direct thrombin inhibitor used instead of heparin in HIT.
glossary.antiphospholipid syndrome: An autoimmune clotting disorder needing lifelong warfarin after VTE.
glossary.Virchow's triad: Venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability: the three causes of thrombosis.
glossary.provoked PE: A PE with an identifiable trigger such as surgery, travel or pregnancy.

technique.stem: A 39 year old woman has sudden breathlessness and sharp left-sided chest pain that is worse on deep breathing. She flew back from Hong Kong 4 days ago and takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her left calf has been aching for 2 days. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. Her chest is clear on auscultation.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about acute pleuritic chest pain.

clues: flew back from Hong Kong 4 days ago
steps.x: Two **VTE risk factors**, calf symptoms, sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia and **hypoxia with a clear chest**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Calf then chest after a flight on the pill: **pulmonary embolism**.

elim: Pericarditis pain eases sitting forward and does not cause hypoxia like this.
Pneumonia evolves over days with productive cough and crackles; the chest is clear.
Musculoskeletal pain does not cause tachycardia and hypoxia.
Pneumothorax gives reduced breath sounds on one side, not a clear chest and calf pain.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary embolism.** Rule: risk factor + sudden pleuritic pain + hypoxia + clear chest = PE.

technique.stem: A 56 year old man has sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain 10 days after a right knee replacement. His right calf is swollen and tender. His pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. PE is the most likely diagnosis. His renal function is normal and he has no allergies.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: Diagnostic test for suspected PE: calculate the Wells score.

clues: 10 days after a right knee replacement
right calf is swollen and tender
PE is the most likely diagnosis
steps.x: DVT signs 3 + PE most likely 3 + HR >100 1.5 + recent surgery 1.5 = **9: PE likely**. Nothing stops contrast.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Wells >4 with no contraindication: **CTPA**.

elim: CXR is usually normal in PE; it excludes other causes but cannot diagnose PE.
D-dimer is for Wells ≤4; it cannot exclude PE when probability is high.
Echo shows RV strain but is for the unstable patient, not the diagnostic test here.
V/Q is for when CTPA is unsuitable: pregnancy, AKI or iodine allergy.

steps.x: **B. CTPA.** Rule: Wells >4 = CTPA; V/Q only if CTPA unsuitable.

technique.stem: A 68 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer on chemotherapy has breathlessness. CTPA shows a segmental pulmonary embolism. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her renal function is normal and she has no bleeding history.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management: choose the drug, then the duration.
**Active cancer**, haemodynamically stable, DOAC suitable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cancer-associated PE: **DOAC for 6 months**.

elim: Aspirin does not treat VTE.
3 months is for provoked PE without active cancer.
Alteplase is for massive PE with hypotension; she is stable.
Confirmed PE always needs anticoagulation unless contraindicated.

steps.x: **C. DOAC for 6 months.** Rule: active cancer with PE = 6 months.

technique.stem: A 44 year old woman has sudden breathlessness 2 weeks after a hysterectomy. Her pulse rate is 120 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. CTPA confirms a large pulmonary embolism. ECG (see item resources) shows sinus tachycardia with a deep S wave in lead I, a Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III, and T inversion in V1–V3.

visual.title: ECG
visual.caption: Sinus tachycardia, T inversion in III and V1–V3.

technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these ECG changes?

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain the ECG in a confirmed PE.

clues: deep S wave in lead I
inverted T wave in lead III
steps.x: **S1Q3T3** plus T inversion over the right ventricle (V1–V3) in a large PE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sudden rise in pulmonary resistance: **acute RV strain**.

elim: Hyperkalaemia gives peaked T waves and wide QRS.
LVH gives tall left-sided voltages and lateral strain.
Pericarditis gives widespread saddle ST elevation.
RCA occlusion gives inferior ST elevation, not this pattern after surgery.

steps.x: **A. Acute right ventricular strain.** Rule: S1Q3T3 and V1–V3 T inversion = RV strain.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has sudden breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain 3 weeks after a caesarean section. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Postpartum, sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest and normal CXR is PE. A slightly raised troponin reflects RV strain, not an MI.

steps.x: Diagnosis of sudden pleuritic chest pain.
**Postpartum** after surgery, sudden pleuritic pain, hypoxia, clear chest, CXR clear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pulmonary embolism**.

elim: Pneumonia would show crackles and consolidation.
Musculoskeletal pain does not cause hypoxia.
Pericarditis is positional and does not cause hypoxia.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy gives heart failure: orthopnoea, crackles, oedema on CXR.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary embolism.** Rule: postpartum + sudden pleuritic pain + hypoxia + normal CXR = PE.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has sudden breathlessness 2 weeks after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. His left calf is swollen. His pulse rate is 112 bpm, BP 130/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. CTPA later confirms a pulmonary embolism.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG?
practice.e: The most common ECG finding in PE is sinus tachycardia. S1Q3T3 is the classic textbook sign but is much less common.

steps.x: 'Most likely' ECG finding: the commonest, not the most famous.
Confirmed PE with a **HR of 112**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sinus tachycardia**.

elim: AF can occur with PE but is far less common.
LBBB is not a feature of PE.
S1Q3T3 is classic but uncommon; the trap answer.
Anterior ST elevation means STEMI, not PE.

steps.x: **D. Sinus tachycardia.** Rule: most common ECG in PE = sinus tachycardia.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain 5 days after a long-haul flight. CTPA confirms bilateral pulmonary emboli. She is breathing fast. An arterial blood gas is taken breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely arterial blood gas finding?
o: Low PaO2 and low PaCO2 (respiratory alkalosis)
Metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap
Metabolic alkalosis with a raised bicarbonate
practice.e: V/Q mismatch causes hypoxaemia, and hyperventilation lowers PaCO2, giving a respiratory alkalosis with a low PaO2. A raised PaCO2 would mean exhaustion or another cause.

steps.x: Predict the ABG in PE.
V/Q mismatch and **hyperventilation**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low PaO2, low PaCO2: **respiratory alkalosis**.

elim: Lactic acidosis only appears in shock; she is not shocked.
Nothing here causes bicarbonate retention.
Bilateral PE with tachypnoea will not give a normal gas.
A raised PaCO2 means hypoventilation, the opposite of what PE causes.

steps.x: **A. Low PaO2 and low PaCO2.** Rule: PE = low O2, low CO2, respiratory alkalosis.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man collapses on the ward 8 days after a hip fracture repair. His pulse rate is 134 bpm, BP 78/48 mmHg for 25 minutes despite fluids, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% on 15 L oxygen. His JVP is raised and his chest is clear. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: ECG
visual.caption: Sinus tachycardia with T inversion in III and V1–V3.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Post-op collapse with persistent hypotension, hypoxia, raised JVP, a clear chest and RV strain on ECG is a massive PE. Tension pneumothorax would give absent breath sounds on one side.

steps.x: Diagnosis of shock after surgery.

clues: 8 days after a hip fracture repair
steps.x: Post-op, **hypotension >15 minutes**, severe hypoxia, raised JVP, clear chest, RV strain ECG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Obstructive shock: **massive PE**.

elim: Tamponade gives muffled heart sounds and small complexes, with no reason here.
Cardiogenic shock from MI gives ST elevation and pulmonary oedema with crackles.
Sepsis gives fever, warm peripheries and a low JVP.
Tension pneumothorax gives unilateral absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation.

steps.x: **C. Massive PE.** Rule: post-op collapse + hypoxia + raised JVP + clear chest = massive PE.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman has a pulmonary embolism confirmed on CTPA. She has not travelled, had surgery or taken oestrogen. She has had three miscarriages and a DVT 2 years ago. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her PE?
practice.e: Recurrent VTE, recurrent miscarriage, mild thrombocytopenia and a prolonged APTT (lupus anticoagulant) point to antiphospholipid syndrome. Factor V Leiden does not prolong the APTT or lower platelets.

steps.x: The cause behind an unprovoked PE.

clues: not travelled, had surgery or taken oestrogen
steps.x: Recurrent VTE + recurrent miscarriage + **low platelets** + **prolonged APTT**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Antiphospholipid syndrome**.

elim: Factor V Leiden does not prolong the APTT or lower platelets.
Nephrotic syndrome needs oedema and proteinuria.
Polycythaemia vera raises haemoglobin, often with high platelets.
Protein C deficiency does not prolong the APTT.

steps.x: **A. Antiphospholipid syndrome.** Rule: VTE + miscarriages + long APTT = APS; treat with lifelong warfarin.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman is being treated with unfractionated heparin for a pulmonary embolism. On day 7 she develops a painful swollen left arm. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her low platelet count?
practice.e: A platelet fall of more than half about a week into heparin with a new thrombosis is HIT. Stop heparin and switch to argatroban with haematology input.

steps.x: Cause of new thrombocytopenia during PE treatment.
Heparin for 7 days, platelets fallen by over 50%, **new thrombosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HIT**: stop heparin, switch to argatroban.

elim: DIC needs a trigger like sepsis, with bleeding and deranged clotting.
ITP causes bleeding, not new thrombosis, and is not timed to heparin.
TTP has haemolytic anaemia, fever, renal and neuro signs; her Hb is normal.
Vitamin K deficiency raises the INR; it does not lower platelets.

steps.x: **B. HIT.** Rule: heparin 5–10 days + platelets halve + new clot = HIT.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man has 2 days of mild pleuritic chest pain after a game of football. He has no leg swelling, haemoptysis or previous VTE. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. An alternative diagnosis is as likely as PE. His 2-level Wells score is 0.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation for pulmonary embolism?
practice.e: A Wells score of 4 or less means PE unlikely, so D-dimer comes first: negative excludes PE, positive leads to CTPA.

steps.x: First test for possible PE: use the Wells score.

clues: An alternative diagnosis is as likely as PE
steps.x: **Wells 0 = PE unlikely.**

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **D-dimer** first.

elim: CTPA first is for Wells >4, or after a positive D-dimer.
Echo is for the unstable patient.
Troponin does not diagnose PE.
V/Q is for when CTPA is needed but unsuitable.

steps.x: **B. D-dimer.** Rule: Wells ≤4 = D-dimer; negative = PE excluded.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain 9 days after a bowel resection. His right calf is swollen. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. His 2-level Wells score is 9.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: PE is likely (Wells 9) but he has an acute kidney injury, so iodinated contrast for CTPA is unsuitable; a V/Q scan is used instead.

steps.x: Diagnostic imaging for PE: check for reasons to avoid CTPA.
**PE likely**, and creatinine has tripled in a week: **AKI**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CTPA unsuitable in AKI: **V/Q scan**.

elim: CTPA contrast risks worsening his AKI.
D-dimer cannot exclude PE when Wells is above 4.
Echo supports RV strain but does not confirm PE in a stable patient.
MR angiography is not a standard PE test.

steps.x: **E. V/Q scan.** Rule: CTPA unsuitable (pregnancy, AKI, iodine allergy) = V/Q.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman has a confirmed pulmonary embolism. Twenty minutes after arrival her pulse rate is 136 bpm, BP 80/50 mmHg despite fluids, and oxygen saturation 86% on 15 L oxygen. She has no history of bleeding, stroke or recent surgery.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Persistent hypotension makes this a massive PE: thrombolyse with IV alteplase (plus IV UFH). Embolectomy is reserved for when thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails.

steps.x: Initial management of an unstable PE.

clues: no history of bleeding, stroke or recent surgery
steps.x: **Massive PE** with no thrombolysis contraindications.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thrombolysis: IV alteplase** (with IV UFH).

elim: Embolectomy is second choice, for when thrombolysis is unsuitable.
A DOAC is for stable PE.
LMWH is too slow and not for massive PE.
Heparin alone stops new clot but does not clear the obstruction.

steps.x: **B. IV alteplase.** Rule: PE + hypotension = thrombolyse.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has a small pulmonary embolism confirmed on CTPA after a long-haul flight. He feels well and wants to go home. His pulse rate is 84 bpm, BP 132/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His PESI score is class I.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: A stable PE with PESI class I–II can be treated as an outpatient with rivaroxaban. Warfarin alone is wrong because it needs LMWH cover at the start.

steps.x: Setting and drug for a stable PE.
Stable, **low-risk PESI**, normal kidneys.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Outpatient rivaroxaban**.

elim: Alteplase is only for massive PE.
UFH is for renal failure or alongside thrombolysis.
A confirmed PE must be anticoagulated.
Warfarin needs LMWH for at least 5 days until INR 2–3.

steps.x: **D. Outpatient rivaroxaban.** Rule: PESI 1–2 = home on rivaroxaban.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man on haemodialysis for end-stage renal failure has a pulmonary embolism confirmed on V/Q scan. He is haemodynamically stable with a pulse rate of 94 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
practice.e: In severe renal insufficiency or ESRF, unfractionated heparin is used because it is not renally cleared and can be monitored and reversed. DOACs and fondaparinux accumulate in renal failure.

steps.x: Anticoagulant choice in a special case.
**ESRF**: avoid renally cleared drugs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Unfractionated heparin**.

elim: Apixaban is first-line only with adequate renal function.
Dabigatran is mostly renally cleared.
Fondaparinux accumulates in renal failure.
Rivaroxaban is avoided in ESRF.

steps.x: **E. UFH.** Rule: severe renal failure = unfractionated heparin.

practice.stem: A 48 year old woman has sudden breathlessness after a long-haul flight. CTPA confirms a pulmonary embolism. Her chest X-ray is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypoxaemia?
o: Diffusion limitation across a thickened membrane
practice.e: The clot leaves lung units ventilated but unperfused: V/Q mismatch. Hypoventilation would raise the PaCO2, but hers is low.

steps.x: Mechanism of low oxygen in PE.
Blocked perfusion with normal lungs; the ABG shows a **low PaCO2**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **V/Q mismatch**.

elim: Hypoventilation would raise PaCO2; hers is low.
Diffusion limitation is fibrosis, with an abnormal CXR.
She is breathing air at normal altitude.
A cardiac shunt is not described; the clot is in the lungs.

steps.x: **E. V/Q mismatch.** Rule: PE = ventilated but unperfused lung.
